claim: Electrotaxis is important in regeneration, development, and wound healing.
source: Electrotaxis, the directional migration of cells in a constant electric field, is important in regeneration, development, and wound healing.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Cortese et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2006)

claim: Electrotaxis has a slower response and a smaller dynamic range than guidance by other cues.
source: Electrotaxis has a slower response and a smaller dynamic range than guidance by other cues, suggesting that the mechanism of electrotaxis shares both similarities and differences with chemical-gradient-sensing pathways.
evidence: Supported by citations and established knowledge about chemotaxis and electrotaxis response characteristics

claim: Electric fields cause several key signaling molecules to be distributed asymmetrically across cells.
source: EFs have been shown to cause several key signaling molecules to be distributed asymmetrically across cells (Sato et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2002; Zhao et al., 2006), setting up cell polarity.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The range of EF strengths sensed by cells is one order of magnitude.
source: The one-order-of-magnitude range of EF strengths sensed by cells (Zhao et al., 2002) is considerably smaller than the four-orders-of-magnitude concentration sensitivity in chemotaxis (Harvath, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The concentration sensitivity in chemotaxis spans four orders of magnitude.
source: The one-order-of-magnitude range of EF strengths sensed by cells (Zhao et al., 2002) is considerably smaller than the four-orders-of-magnitude concentration sensitivity in chemotaxis (Harvath, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Cells respond to chemical guidance cues on a time scale of seconds.
source: Furthermore, whereas cells respond to chemical guidance cues on a time scale of seconds and develop polarity over several minutes, the response to an EF can take up to 10 min or more after the EF is turned on Wang et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2006.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Cells develop polarity in response to chemical cues over several minutes.
source: Furthermore, whereas cells respond to chemical guidance cues on a time scale of seconds and develop polarity over several minutes, the response to an EF can take up to 10 min or more after the EF is turned on Wang et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2006.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The response to an electric field can take up to 10 min or more after the EF is turned on.
source: Furthermore, whereas cells respond to chemical guidance cues on a time scale of seconds and develop polarity over several minutes, the response to an EF can take up to 10 min or more after the EF is turned on Wang et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2006.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: Actin polymerization coordinated with its associated signaling molecules self-organizes into microscale spatial regions that travel as waves across plasma membranes.
source: Actin polymerization, coordinated with its associated signaling molecules, self-organizes into microscale spatial regions that travel as waves across plasma membranes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of cortical wave systems

claim: Cortical waves drive various cell behaviors, such as migration and division.
source: These waves drive various cell behaviors, such as migration and division (Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Bretschneider et al., 2009; Flemming et al., 2020; Gerhardt et al., 2014; Gerisch, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: The wave system can be described as a coupled signal-transduction excitable network – cytoskeletal excitable network (STEN-CEN).
source: The wave system can be described as a coupled signal-transduction excitable network – cytoskeletal excitable network (STEN-CEN) (Devreotes et al., 2017; Miao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: STEN-CEN has the characteristics of an excitable system, including exhibiting an activation threshold for wave initiation and experiencing refractory periods.
source: STEN-CEN has the characteristics of an excitable system, including exhibiting an activation threshold for wave initiation and experiencing refractory periods.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of excitable systems

claim: STEN-CEN wave properties dictate protrusion properties.
source: It has been shown that the STEN-CEN wave properties dictate protrusion properties (Miao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Tuning the activity levels of key components in STEN-CEN changes wave patterns, which leads to the transition of protrusion profiles.
source: Tuning the activity levels of key components in STEN-CEN changes wave patterns, which leads to the transition of protrusion profiles.
evidence: Based on inference from prior studies

claim: An activator/inhibitor, reaction/diffusion system model successfully recapitulates the experimental results.
source: An activator/inhibitor, reaction/diffusion system model successfully recapitulates the experimental results (Bhattacharya et al., 2020; Bhattacharya and Iglesias, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: In many cell types that show a strong response to EFs, the wave area is comparable to the cell area.
source: One challenge in investigating whether cortical waves can act as the mediators of EFs is that in many of the cell types that show a strong response to EFs, the wave area is comparable to the cell area.
evidence: Based on observation and established knowledge

claim: Waves are generated at the leading edge of the cell during directed migration.
source: Furthermore, waves are generated at the leading edge of the cell during directed migration (Xu et al., 2003), so that wave dynamics are tightly coupled with cell dynamics.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Wave dynamics are tightly coupled with cell dynamics.
source: Furthermore, waves are generated at the leading edge of the cell during directed migration (Xu et al., 2003), so that wave dynamics are tightly coupled with cell dynamics.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that waves are generated at the leading edge

claim: Electro-fused giant D. discoideum cells have diameters up to ten times larger than that of an individual cell.

claim: Multiple simultaneous waves can be generated across the surface contact area of a giant cell.
source: Multiple simultaneous waves can be generated across the surface contact area of a giant cell (Gerhardt et al., 2014).

claim: Giant cell waves generate actin-filled macropinosomes on the dorsal membrane.
source: These waves also generate actin-filled macropinosomes on the dorsal membrane (Veltman et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Upon contact with nanotopography, cells produce quasi-1D wave patches.
source: Upon contact with nanotopography, cells produce quasi-1D wave patches.

claim: The phenomenon of guided actin polymerization by nanotopography is known as esotaxis.
source: The phenomenon of guided actin polymerization by nanotopography is known as esotaxis (Driscoll et al., 2014), and has been investigated in detail (Ketchum et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2020).

claim: Waves persist for a shorter time on nanotopography than on flat surfaces.
source: First, these waves persist for a shorter time on nanotopography than on flat surfaces, enabling us to investigate whether wave systems with different characteristic timescales respond to EFs differently.

claim: Due to the shorter lifetime, waves on ridged surfaces only propagate in local regions of giant cells.
source: Second, due to the shorter lifetime, waves on ridged surfaces only propagate in local regions of giant cells.
evidence: Based on experimental observation

claim: In single, differentiated cells, usually only one wave is generated at the leading edge.
source: In single, differentiated cells, usually only one wave is generated at the leading edge (Figure 1a and Video 1), and the wave motion is coupled with cell motion.

claim: In single cells, the wave motion is coupled with cell motion.
source: In single, differentiated cells, usually only one wave is generated at the leading edge (Figure 1a and Video 1), and the wave motion is coupled with cell motion.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1a and Video 1

claim: When a single cell changes its direction of motion, the wave remains at the leading edge.
source: For instance, when the cell in Figure 1a changed its direction of motion, the wave remained at the leading edge (72 s - 120 s).

claim: In giant cells, multiple waves were initiated randomly and propagated radially across the basal membranes.
source: In giant cells, multiple waves were initiated randomly and propagated radially across the basal membranes (Figure 1b and Video 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1b and Video 2

claim: CEN is driven by STEN, but has a substantially shorter characteristic timescale.
source: CEN is driven by STEN, but has a substantially shorter characteristic timescale.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the STEN-CEN system

claim: PIP3 waves displayed band-like shapes, whereas F-actin appeared across the bands with higher levels at the rims of PIP3 waves.
source: Thus, PIP3 waves displayed band-like shapes, whereas F-actin appeared across the bands with higher levels at the rims of PIP3 waves (Miao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study

claim: Colliding waves did not cross, but instead rotated by 90°.
source: As shown in Figure 1b, colliding waves did not cross, but instead rotated by 90° (Figure 1b , 150 s - 200 s).

source: This behavior is suggestive of a refractory period following excitation, which is a hallmark of an excitable system.

claim: On nanoridges, giant cells generated multiple, quasi-1D patches of F-actin and PIP3 with shorter lifetimes than on flat surfaces.
source: On nanoridges, the giant cells generated multiple, quasi-1D patches of F-actin and PIP3 with shorter lifetimes than on flat surfaces (Figure 1c and Video 3).

claim: Some waves on nanoridges formed and propagated for a short distance, whereas others formed and then quickly dissipated.

claim: Wave dissipation can be explained in terms of an excitable system with lateral inhibition, in which the dispersion of the inhibitor is faster than that of the activator.
source: The wave dissipation can be explained in terms of an excitable system with lateral inhibition, in which the dispersion of the inhibitor is faster than that of the activator.

claim: In an excitable system with lateral inhibition, the waves eventually dissipate due to the spatial accumulation of the inhibitor.
source: Thus, the waves eventually dissipate due to the spatial accumulation of the inhibitor.
evidence: Based on inference from theoretical models

claim: In an excitable system with lateral inhibition, the excitable system threshold determines the wave duration.
source: Prior studies have shown that in this situation, the excitable system threshold determines the wave duration (Bhattacharya et al., 2020; Ermentrout et al., 1984).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies

claim: 1D patches on nanoridges occurred throughout the basal surfaces, and thus were independent of cell motion.
source: As was the case on flat surfaces, 1D patches occurred throughout the basal surfaces on ridges, and thus were independent of cell motion.
evidence: Based on experimental observation

claim: Waves were also generated on the dorsal planes.
source: Waves were also generated on the dorsal planes.
evidence: Based on experimental observation

claim: In contrast to basal waves, which propagated across the surface contact, dorsal waves were associated with membrane deformations, and resembled macropinosomes.
source: In contrast to basal waves, which propagated across the surface contact (Videos 2 and 3), dorsal waves were associated with membrane deformations, and resembled macropinosomes (Video 4).

claim: Dorsal waves were primarily generated in cuplike structures, whereas the stripe-like basal waves spanned the entire basal plane.

evidence: Based on experimental observation

claim: PIP3 activity was coordinated with F-actin activity both in the absence and presence of an EF.

claim: Giant cells respond to a narrow range (15 V/cm to 20 V/cm) of EF amplitudes.

source: We found that giant cells respond to a narrow range (15 V/cm to 20 V/cm) of EF amplitudes (Videos 7 and 8), and that higher voltage (35 V/cm) damaged cells.

claim: In the absence of an EF, individual actin polymerization events were initiated in patches on the basal surfaces.
source: In the absence of an EF (top row in Figure 2a), individual actin polymerization events were initiated in patches on the basal surfaces (Figure 2a and Video 9).

claim: In the first several minutes after turning on the EF, most patches propagated as a wave along a single ridge.
source: In the first several minutes after turning on the EF, most patches propagated as a wave along a single ridge (Figure 2a, blue inset).

source: After the EF was on for 10 min, some patches appeared to undergo coordinated motion across several ridges (Figure 2a, pink inset).

claim: Actin patches were larger in the presence of an EF and organized into larger groups located preferentially at the cell front.

claim: Larger actin patches at cell fronts lead to wider protrusions at cell fronts that drove directed cell migration.
source: Actin patches were larger in the presence of an EF and organized into larger groups located preferentially at the cell front (bottom row in Figure 2a, 20 min, and 25 min), leading to wider protrusions at cell fronts that drove directed cell migration (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).

claim: Density scatter plots of wave dimensions parallel and perpendicular to ridges exhibit elliptical contours.

source: This difference is consistent with the EF drawing the system closer to the excitability threshold.
